how_it_works.text: Chandra uses four nested pairs of grazing-incidence mirrors, coated with iridium, to deflect X-rays that would otherwise pass straight through or be absorbed. The mirror shells focus incoming photons onto a 9.2-metre optical bench, where either the ACIS CCD camera or the HRC microchannel-plate detector records an image, while the HETGS and LETG gratings spread the X-rays into spectra. Because Earth's atmosphere blocks X-rays, the observatory flies in a highly elliptical orbit that reaches roughly 139,000 km above the surface.

why_important.text: Chandra was the first X-ray telescope to deliver sub-arcsecond imaging, letting astronomers resolve structures that earlier missions could only blur together. It has mapped million-degree gas in galaxy clusters, traced shock fronts in supernova remnants, measured matter falling toward black holes, and shown how dark matter separates from ordinary gas during cluster collisions. Those observations underpin much of modern high-energy astrophysics and complement the infrared and visible-light work of Hubble and Webb.

status.text: NASA lists Chandra as an active mission as of the agency page's 14 April 2026 update. The Chandra X-ray Center, operated for NASA by the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory, continues to run flight operations and science activities, and the observatory remains in its highly elliptical orbit.

how_it_works.text: Clementine was built around a small, lightweight bus and carried 15 advanced flight-test components alongside nine science instruments. Its lunar mapping payload combined an ultraviolet/visible camera, a near-infrared camera and a laser altimeter, which together recorded surface colour, mineral signatures and topography. Two further cameras served as star trackers for the spacecraft's autonomous attitude system. The Naval Research Laboratory designed, integrated and flew the spacecraft for the Ballistic Missile Defense Organization, while NASA provided science oversight and investigators.

why_important.text: Clementine produced the first near-global multispectral map of the Moon and the first global topographic map from lunar orbit, giving scientists a consistent data set for studying the crust's composition and relief. Its bistatic radar experiment returned signals consistent with water ice trapped in a permanently shadowed crater near the south pole, a result that reshaped lunar polar science and motivated later ice-hunting missions. The project also became an early template for the 'faster, better, cheaper' approach that shaped NASA's Discovery programme.

status.text: Clementine's mission ended on 8 August 1994, after a thruster fault and a power-system failure prevented the planned Geographos flyby and drained the spacecraft's battery. Lunar gravity had already pushed it into a heliocentric orbit on 20 July 1994, and controllers briefly regained contact between 20 February and 10 May 1995. The spacecraft has not been operated since.

how_it_works.text: CloudSat carried a single instrument, the Cloud Profiling Radar, a nadir-pointing 94 GHz W-band radar that measured the strength of backscattered pulses at successive heights through a cloud. That produced vertical slices of cloud structure with about 500 m resolution, revealing where liquid water, ice and precipitation sit inside a cloud rather than only how its top appears. The spacecraft flew in a 705 km, 98.2-degree sun-synchronous orbit as part of the A-Train, and had a launch mass of 847 kg.

why_important.text: CloudSat was the first satellite to profile the vertical structure of clouds across the globe, filling a gap previously covered only by cloud-top imagers and ground-based radars. Its measurements of cloud water content, snowfall and precipitation helped test and improve the cloud parameterisations used in climate and weather models. The mission's long global record continues to support studies of how cloud systems vary with season, region and climate.

status.text: NASA decommissioned CloudSat on 20 December 2023, when radar science operations concluded. The spacecraft completed final orbit-lowering manoeuvres and was passivated in April 2024, leaving it inactive and awaiting disposal. Its radar data remain archived and continue to be used for climate and weather research.

how_it_works.text: Cluster II is a set of four identical spinning spacecraft that fly in a tetrahedral formation, so the same region of near-Earth space is sampled at four points at once. Their orbits are highly eccentric and near-polar, with a nominal perigee of about 4 Earth radii, apogee of about 19.6 Earth radii, a period near 57 hours and an inclination of about 90.7 degrees. Each spacecraft carries a matched suite of magnetometers, electric-field sensors, wave receivers and particle spectrometers, and the separation between the four is adjusted to match the scale of the plasma structures being studied.

why_important.text: Before Cluster, most magnetospheric measurements came from single spacecraft, which could not separate spatial structure from temporal change. Flying four identical observatories in a known formation let researchers resolve boundaries, currents, waves and turbulence in three dimensions and trace how solar-wind energy enters Earth's magnetosphere. The mission operated for more than two decades, supported space-weather modelling, and ended with the first repeated targeted reentries of a multi-spacecraft science constellation.

status.text: Cluster's science operations are complete. The four satellites were disposed of through targeted reentries over the South Pacific: Salsa on 8 September 2024, Rumba on 22 October 2025, Samba on 31 August 2026 and Tango on 1 September 2026. ESA describes the campaign as the first repeated, controlled reentry of a multi-spacecraft science mission.

how_it_works.text: Curiosity is a car-sized rover that landed in Gale Crater using a rocket-powered descent stage, which lowered it to the surface on a tether before flying away. It moves on six wheels with a rocker-bogie suspension and draws power from a radioisotope thermoelectric generator rather than solar panels. Its instruments include the SAM and CheMin laboratories for analysing drilled rock powder, the ChemCam laser spectrometer and Mastcam cameras on the mast, the APXS and MAHLI sensors on the robotic arm, and the DAN, REMS and RAD environment instruments.

why_important.text: Curiosity's central question was whether Gale Crater ever offered conditions that could have supported microbial life. The mission established that the crater once held a long-lived freshwater lake with the chemical ingredients and energy sources needed for life, detected complex organic molecules in ancient mudstones, and documented how Martian climate and habitability changed over time. Its radiation and weather measurements also inform planning for human exploration.

status.text: Curiosity remains active in Gale Crater. NASA reported on 26 August 2026 that the rover had gained about 1 km of elevation during its climb of Mount Sharp, and the mission continues to study progressively younger sedimentary layers.

how_it_works.text: CYGNSS uses eight small observatories in low Earth orbit, each carrying a Delay Doppler Mapping Instrument that listens for GPS signals reflected from the ocean surface. The shape and strength of the reflected signal depend on surface roughness, which is used to retrieve wind speed beneath the storm. Each satellite uses under 60 W of power and weighs less than 30 kg, deploying solar panels after launch, and the constellation's orbits are arranged to revisit tropical storms frequently.

why_important.text: CYGNSS was designed to measure ocean surface winds inside tropical cyclones, where heavy rain and cloud tops block or obscure visible and infrared images. By flying a constellation of small satellites, it increases the number of observations of a storm's inner core and helps forecasters track intensification, complementing larger weather satellites and aircraft reconnaissance.

status.text: CYGNSS is listed by NASA as an active mission and continues to operate in extended mission. Its data are used in research on tropical cyclones, ocean surface winds and air-sea exchange.

how_it_works.text: Danuri, also called the Korea Pathfinder Lunar Orbiter, is a 678 kg spacecraft about 1.8 by 2.1 by 2.3 m in size. It reached the Moon on a ballistic lunar transfer that uses solar, Earth and lunar gravity rather than a direct braking burn, then entered a 100 km circular polar orbit. Its six payloads include Korean cameras, a magnetometer and a gamma-ray spectrometer, together with NASA's ShadowCam, which is sensitive enough to image permanently shadowed polar terrain using light reflected from nearby crater walls.

why_important.text: Danuri is the Republic of Korea's first mission beyond Earth orbit and its first lunar orbiter. It gives Korean engineers and scientists operational experience in lunar trajectory design, deep-space communications and payload operations, while its imagery, magnetic and gamma-ray data add to international lunar datasets. ShadowCam's images of permanently shadowed regions support planning for future polar landings, including Artemis.

status.text: Danuri is active. KARI states that the mission was extended by two years and is scheduled to continue science operations through 2027.

how_it_works.text: Dawn used three 30 cm xenon ion thrusters, derived from the engine flown on Deep Space 1, as its main propulsion. The thrusters ionise xenon and accelerate it electrostatically, producing up to about 92 mN of thrust at 2.6 kW with a specific impulse between 1900 and 3200 seconds, so the spacecraft could change orbit around Vesta and Ceres using very little propellant. Two 2.3 by 8.3 m solar arrays supplied up to 10.3 kW at 1 AU, and a 35 Ah nickel-hydrogen battery carried the spacecraft through eclipse.

why_important.text: Dawn was the first spacecraft to orbit two separate extraterrestrial bodies, Vesta and Ceres, and the first to use ion propulsion to do so. At Vesta it showed a differentiated protoplanet with a basaltic crust and huge impact basins; at Ceres it found a water-ice-rich crust, bright carbonate deposits and evidence of briny material reaching the surface. Together the two encounters let scientists compare how a rocky inner-belt body and an ice-rich dwarf planet evolved.

status.text: Dawn's mission ended on 1 November 2018, when the spacecraft exhausted its hydrazine. It remains in orbit around Ceres, where it is expected to stay for decades.

how_it_works.text: Deep Impact flew two connected spacecraft: a 370 kg copper impactor and a 650 kg flyby bus. The impactor was released about 24 hours before encounter and struck comet Tempel 1 at 10.2 km/s, while the flyby watched from a safe distance with its High Resolution Instrument, Medium Resolution Instrument and infrared spectrometer. The copper mass was chosen so that the impactor's own material would not confuse measurements of the comet's composition.

why_important.text: The collision excavated material from beneath Tempel 1's surface, allowing the flyby to analyse fresh cometary ice, dust and organic compounds and to watch how a crater forms on a low-gravity body. The experiment produced the first direct look inside a comet nucleus and linked the mission to later studies of cometary structure and the delivery of volatiles to the inner solar system.

status.text: Deep Impact's primary mission ended after the Tempel 1 encounter, and the spacecraft was then reused as EPOXI for a flyby of comet Hartley 2 in 2010 and other observations. NASA lost contact with the spacecraft on 16 September 2013 and declared the mission complete.

how_it_works.text: Deep Space 1 was built around a xenon ion propulsion system that used electricity from solar arrays to accelerate ions and produce a very small but continuous thrust. The 30 cm engine carried about 81.5 kg of xenon, and the spacecraft's total launch mass was 486.3 kg. It also flew an autonomous navigation package, AutoNav, that used camera images of asteroids and stars to steer the spacecraft without ground intervention, plus the MICAS camera/spectrometer and the PEPE plasma instrument.

why_important.text: Deep Space 1 was a technology demonstration that proved ion propulsion could serve as a primary deep-space propulsion system, and it validated autonomous optical navigation and miniaturised science instruments. Its encounters with asteroid Braille and comet Borrelly showed that these technologies could deliver real science, and the ion engine design became the basis for the propulsion used on Dawn.

status.text: Deep Space 1 completed its mission on 18 December 2001, after the Borrelly flyby. The spacecraft was intentionally shut down and remains inactive in heliocentric orbit.

how_it_works.text: DSCOVR orbits the Sun-Earth L1 point about 1.5 million km sunward of Earth, where it can sample the solar wind before it reaches the planet. Its PlasMag suite combines a Faraday cup and a magnetometer to measure the speed, density, temperature and magnetic field of the incoming plasma. A pair of Earth-viewing instruments, EPIC and NISTAR, look back at the fully illuminated Earth to image the disk and measure reflected sunlight and emitted radiation.

why_important.text: DSCOVR is NOAA's operational real-time solar-wind monitor and the successor to NASA's ACE at L1. Its measurements give forecasters roughly 15 to 60 minutes of warning before a solar-wind disturbance reaches Earth, supporting geomagnetic storm watches and alerts that protect satellites, power grids, aviation and GPS users. EPIC's images also provide a continuous view of the sunlit Earth for climate and cloud studies.

status.text: DSCOVR is listed by NASA as an active mission and continues to operate at L1 under NOAA. NOAA took over routine operations on 28 October 2015.
